Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.

As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.

Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.

Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).

We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.

### Memory notes

By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).

In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.

Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?

### Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need

Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.

Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0 , a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.

Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.

We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents . Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next.

Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.

Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.

Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).

Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.

### Claude has learned to judge salience

We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red , a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).

We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).

Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md , and earned four badges.

Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.

Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.

Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”

With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.

### Steering Claude to write memory

We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).

We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.

We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.

In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.

With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.

### Dreaming can correct memory

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.

Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.

In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.

At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.

We then tested whether dreaming could help Claude avoid this trap. We ran dreaming on the memory folder that contained the wrong location for the PokéCenter: Claude checked the note against the session transcript, caught its error, and rewrote it. The transcript gave Claude a ground truth to validate its memory against. With the corrected memory note, Claude went straight back into Mt. Moon and eventually reached Cerulean City.

In the run with the uncorrected note, Claude dropped back onto that earlier route three times. After the third failure, Claude seemed to give up, writing, “I’m going to stop rather than keep looping.” Our setup’s automatic reply instructed it to continue. So it did, all the way back to Pewter City, the town before the mountain, where it hoped to heal and restock. The run ended without Claude ever reaching Cerulean City.

### 01 Summary

Johannes Hermle*, Ben Jones*, Lukas Althoff*, Ryan Heller, Thomas Lyttelton, Carolyn Stein, Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory

*Lead authors of the report

## Summary

- What we measure. AI could speed up scientific discovery, but by how much depends on what AI can do and how scientists use it. Using privacy-preserving methods, we study 207,000 Claude and Claude Code research sessions to understand how Claude is used across scientific fields and research tasks. We are conducting this research to help the public better understand the state of AI for science today and assess the impact that AI may have on scientific discovery in the future.

- Where scientists use Claude. Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an accompanying survey, they rank those tasks as the most important for scientific discovery. That said, specialized AI tools designed for scientific work could narrow the gap between the research tasks scientists use AI for and the ones they consider most important. On Claude Science, for instance, idea generation makes up about twice the share of use that it does on Claude.

- How Claude use tracks AI capability. We create a measure of how well AI can, in theory, perform each research task. The tasks AI is best suited to (the top 20% on this measure) get two to four times as much Claude use as the time researchers spend on them would predict. The tasks AI is least suited to (the bottom 20%), which include most physical work, get very little. We observe the same pattern across fields: fields where AI can perform many tasks well, such as computer science and statistics, use Claude more.

- What this could mean for the speed of scientific discovery. Using a simple model, we explore scenarios for how much AI could speed up research. If existing AI capabilities are widely adopted, they could double research output in some fields. If AI could carry out all non-physical research work, output in fields such as computer science and statistics could rise as much as 15-fold, while output in bench sciences such as chemistry and biology, which are held back by physical bottlenecks, would rise three- or fourfold. In our survey of researchers who actively use AI, about 40% expect AI models to carry out full research projects on their own by 2030.

## Introduction

Science has been described as an “endless frontier” (Bush 1945). But how fast we explore that frontier has historically been limited by a scarce resource: the time and talent of human researchers. Artificial intelligence could ease that limit by amplifying what researchers can do, transforming both the process of discovery and the pace of exploration (Wang et al. 2023; Amodei 2024). Few applications of AI could matter more for human welfare. Given the highly cognitive nature of research compared with most sectors of the economy, AI’s effects may be particularly large and early in this domain.

Recent examples show AI playing a growing role in scientific discovery. In structural biology, AlphaFold predicted the three-dimensional shapes of over 200 million proteins (Jumper et al. 2021; Varadi et al. 2024), and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In materials science, GNoME predicted 380,000 stable new crystals (Merchant et al. 2023). In mathematics, researchers have used AI systems to help resolve decades-old Erdős problems, produce a potential proof for a Millennium Prize problem, and make progress on other major problems, from open conjectures to verifying landmark proofs (Anthropic 2026a, 2026b; OpenAI 2026a, 2026b; Tsoukalas et al. 2026).

Beyond these developments, most scientific progress involves many specialized, interlinked research tasks, which can vary substantially across fields. How much AI accelerates scientific discovery depends not only on AI’s capabilities, but also on how it is adopted across these tasks. In this report, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to study the scientific use of Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Science. We document how usage varies across fields and tasks, identify what explains these usage patterns, and outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate research.

Claude use in science varies by field. Relative to their number of researchers, formal sciences such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics use Claude more heavily, while health and lab-based physical sciences use it less. Across research tasks, scientists use Claude more for analyzing data and writing, and less for gathering data or generating ideas and hypotheses. This is consistent with self-reported AI use from an accompanying survey of scientists.

To understand these differences, we develop a measure of theoretical AI capability. Claude use is higher in tasks and fields that score higher on this measure. These also tend to be more cognitive in nature and better suited to reinforcement learning, in which AI learns from feedback on repeated attempts. In short, scientists appear to use AI where it works best.

Based on these findings, we outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate scientific progress. With current capabilities, research output in some fields could as much as double, primarily from task-level augmentation. Researchers in our survey expect much greater capabilities to come. In a hypothetical scenario where AI fully automates all non-physical work, highly cognitive fields such as computer science or statistics could see up to a 15-fold increase in output. Because the fields with the largest potential for acceleration include those that produce AI itself, these gains could create an additional feedback loop, in which faster AI research produces more capable AI, which in turn could further accelerate research.

While faster scientific discovery could bring substantial benefits to humanity, AI-driven research also carries risks and uncertainties. Less human oversight could lead to the pursuit of dangerous or unethical research. AI could also reshape researchers’ careers, making research work more or less rewarding, and alter the sense of purpose associated with the human pursuit of knowledge.

## How we conducted this research

Our goal with this research is to measure the different ways scientists use Claude while protecting the details of their work. To do this, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to analyze the scientific use of Claude on consumer plans. A language model, used here as a “classifier,” reads each session transcript and labels it with a fixed set of categories, such as the field and the research task it involves, according to a predefined taxonomy (SciNet taxonomy by Alamos and Althoff 2026). The resulting labels, such as “chemistry” or “data cleaning,” are the only information from these conversations retained and analyzed by the research team for this report. No classifier employed in this study extracts and stores open-ended information or details on research content, such as research datasets, hypotheses, experimental methods, early findings, or unpublished papers. Results are reported only in aggregate and only for cells that meet a minimum number of distinct accounts. All classifiers introduced in this study are listed in the Appendix .

Our measurement involves two steps. A first classifier identifies whether a session transcript involves scientific work. A second classifier then assigns each of these transcripts to a field, subfield, and task in the SciNet taxonomy. SciNet contains 7,262 tasks, spanning 34 fields and 318 subfields. Some tasks in the taxonomy, such as drafting manuscripts, are universal to all fields. Others are specific to individual fields or subfields. For instance, in the taxonomy, the task of predicting optical absorption and emission spectra is specific to materials science. Together, the tasks cover the full process of producing a new research finding.

Our main sample consists of 207,049 sessions on consumer plans from August 2 to September 30, 2026, which were assigned a scientific field and a research task: 128,914 from Chat and Cowork, two general-purpose interfaces for conversation and knowledge work, hereafter referred to as “Claude,” and 78,135 from Claude Code, an agentic coding tool that works directly with a user’s files, writing and running code. We also study a supplemental sample of Claude Science sessions. For details on sample construction, see the Appendix .

Combining usage data and a structured taxonomy of research tasks allows us to study which fields adopt Claude and for which parts of the research process. This research contributes to a growing body of work attempting to measure the adoption of AI technology for scientific discovery (Kobak et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025; Hao et al. 2026; Codreanu et al. 2026).

## How Claude use varies across scientific fields

We begin by describing how Claude use varies across scientific fields. Figure 1 compares a field’s share of sessions against the share of global researchers in that field, giving us a sense of relative use per scientific field. 1 On Claude, the three largest fields by session share are computer science (11.9%), engineering (8.4%), and medicine (7.7%), which are also among the largest fields by global researcher counts. 2 Overall, fields with a larger share of researchers also tend to account for a larger share of Claude sessions (log-log correlation of 0.79).

However, Claude use per field cannot be explained by the number of researchers alone. In Figure 1, fields above the 45-degree line show higher usage relative to their size, while fields below the line show lower usage. Relative usage is especially high for the formal sciences, including computer science, mathematics, and statistics. Usage is also high for the social sciences. By contrast, physical sciences such as chemistry, where work often happens in a lab, tend to show lower relative usage. So does medicine, the third-largest field by session volume, where researchers spend much of their time with patients.

On Claude Code, usage is less strongly related to field size (log-log correlation with researcher counts of 0.62) and concentrates in more quantitative fields. Despite making up only 4.3% of the world’s researchers, computer science alone accounts for 32.7% of Claude Code sessions. 3 Other formal sciences, such as mathematics and statistics, also show high relative usage. Relative usage is low in the arts and humanities and in the social sciences, with the exception of economics, a comparatively quantitative field.

We observe similar patterns when comparing usage across 318 subfields within those 34 fields (Figure 2). 4 This more granular subfield view reveals that artificial intelligence and machine learning stands out, with session shares of 5.0% for Claude and 15.2% for Claude Code, despite making up only 1.2% of the world’s researchers. More generally, regardless of the broad scientific domain, computational subfields are among the strongest adopters. These subfields include computational biology, computational linguistics, and computational neuroscience. Robotics also shows high relative usage, likely because it builds heavily on computational methods despite its focus on physical systems.

### Chapter 01 : Executive summary

Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

## Executive summary

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

- Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library. Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6 . Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.

The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

- Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

- The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;

- A technical report explaining the details of our system;

- A (Claude-written) protocol specification document;

- Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and

- Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license. 1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

## Introduction

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference . For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development , in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees , in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators , and more.

## Trust challenges in AI proliferation

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” ( zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge ). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier , by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

### Challenge 1: pacing

Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used . For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information. 2 We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

### Challenge 2: tamper detection

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become prime targets . An attacker or rogue agent may compromise an inference server to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while hiding among genuine responses . The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our Frontier Safety Roadmap , Anthropic set a public goal to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “ We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights. ” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method. 3

How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.
